A graph with 16 vertices, girth at least 8, and 21 edges must have an average degree of 2.625, meaning it has 10 vertices of degree 3 and 6 vertices of degree 2 (to minimize paths of length 2 and 3). Because the girth is 8, there are no cycles of length 7 or less, which implies that all paths of length 1, 2, and 3 between any pair of vertices must be unique and mutually disjoint. 

Counting the minimum number of pairs of vertices at distances 1, 2, and 3 yields 21, 36, and 60 pairs respectively, summing to 117 pairs. Since there are only 120 total pairs of vertices in a 16-vertex graph, almost all vertices must reach each other within 3 steps. 

By expanding the BFS tree from any degree 3 vertex up to level 3, we can calculate the maximum number of vertices it can reach. Due to the required number of degree 2 vertices, the expansion is strictly bottlenecked. Summing the maximum possible reachable vertices at distance <= 3 across all degree 3 vertices yields a strict mathematical contradiction (the theoretical maximum falls short of the required minimum to fit within 16 vertices). Thus, no such graph can exist.
